summary: Team MAJIX built Lunar Sentinel to address the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by connecting three questions: where to land, when to land, and how to stay connected at the Moon’s south pole. We researched terrain, shadow, power, and communication risks, then used NASA LOLA elevation maps, LRO imagery, and JPL Horizons Sun and Earth positions to calculate slopes, terrain horizons, sunlight, and Earth visibility. Our website lets users explore map layers, select locations, inspect five-meter terrain detail at four study sites, and identify useful landing windows. We also developed a proposed relay-satellite simulation to explore reducing communication gaps and a LIDAR demonstration showing how laser sensing could support touchdown decisions. Our creative contribution is linking terrain, timing, and communication to the same selected location in one interactive workflow. We built an offline-capable HTML, CSS, and JavaScript website with a Python data pipeline, implemented 25 automated tests, checked results against NASA products and Apollo 17 conditions, and clearly separated measured data, calculations, and proposals while documenting limitations. The result is a transparent planning and learning prototype—not a flight-certified system—that makes lunar mission trade-offs easier to understand.
details: We’re Team MAJIX, and we built Lunar Sentinel to help people explore three big questions about landing at the Moon’s south pole: where to land, when to land, and how to stay connected to Earth. We used NASA terrain maps, lunar images, and Sun and Earth positions to create a website where users can choose a location, inspect slopes and shadows, and find landing windows with useful sunlight and Earth visibility. We also explored a proposed relay satellite that could reduce communication gaps and created a LIDAR demonstration to explain how laser sensing could help during touchdown. What makes our project creative is that everything stays connected to the same selected location, turning separate datasets into one clear, interactive experience. We developed it with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas, used Python to process the data, and checked our work with 25 automated tests and comparisons against NASA products and Apollo 17 conditions. Throughout development, we considered terrain hazards, power needs, communication outages, data quality, and ease of use. Our goal is to make lunar planning more understandable for students, educators, and people exploring mission ideas, so we made the website work offline and clearly labeled what comes from NASA, what we calculated, and what we proposed. It’s a planning and learning prototype—not a flight-ready system—and we’re honest about its limits, including remaining relay gaps and hazards too small for the maps to show.
